196 FERC ¶ 61,245
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

Before Commissioners:  Laura V. Swett, Chairman;
                                        David Rosner, Lindsay S. See,
                                        Judy W. Chang, and David LaCerte.


ORDER ACCEPTING RELIABILITY BACKSTOP PROCUREMENT AND ESTABLISHING FURTHER PROCEDURES

(Issued September 29, 2026)

On July 31, 2026, as supplemented on August 14, 2026, PJM submitted proposed changes to its Open Access Transmission Tariff (OATT or Tariff) and Reliability Assurance Agreement (RAA), pursuant to section 205 of the Federal Power Act (FPA), to establish the Reliability Backstop Procurement (RBP).  The RBP is a one-time procurement of new capacity to address significant resource adequacy challenges primarily driven by an influx of large loads.  As discussed below, we accept the proposed RBP for filing, suspend it for five months, effective February 28, 2027,    subject to refund, and establish a paper hearing.  We also establish an FPA section 206 proceeding.
We find that certain aspects of PJM’s proposal are just and reasonable.  With respect to other aspects of PJM’s proposal that may be unjust and unreasonable, we direct further briefing regarding potential alternative approaches that the Commission believes may be just and reasonable.  We therefore establish paper hearing procedures and a process by which the Commission may potentially revise those provisions consistent with FPA section 206.  
Recognizing the looming capacity shortfall facing PJM, we encourage PJM to consider the issues we raise in this order and determine the most expeditious path to resolving them.  In particular, we encourage PJM to swiftly submit a new FPA section 205 filing without delay.  That new filing may in turn obviate the need for the paper hearing procedures that we establish here and could expedite a potential RBP auction. 
Background
PJM conducts a Base Residual Auction (BRA) to procure resource commitments sufficient to meet reliability requirements in the PJM region for a given delivery year, which spans from June 1 to May 31.  The BRA and three Incremental Auctions are the Reliability Pricing Model (RPM) Auctions for a given delivery year.
In December 2025, PJM announced that a BRA had cleared significantly below PJM’s reliability requirement for the first time in the auction’s history.  The 2027/2028 BRA cleared 6,623 MW short of the reliability requirement, when also accounting for Fixed Resource Requirement (FRR) resources.  The largest driver of the shortfall was 5,250 MW of load growth forecast for that delivery year, nearly 5,100 MW of which was due to data centers.  The 2027/2028 BRA, which cleared at the temporary price cap of $333.44/MW-day, was the third BRA in a row to clear at historically high prices.
In January 2026, the White House National Energy Dominance Council (NEDC) and the governors of all 13 PJM states released a document titled “Statement of Principles Regarding PJM” (NEDC/PJM Governors’ Principles).  The document urged PJM to file tariff revisions with the Commission to “[p]rovide 15-year price certainty for new capacity resources,” which “can be accomplished by holding a Reliability Backstop Auction to procure new capacity resources commencing no later than September 2026.”  Noting the unique risks data centers pose to resource adequacy, the document urged PJM to allocate the costs of any new capacity procured to load-serving entities with data centers that have not self-procured new capacity or agreed to be curtailable, with any remaining costs allocated to load-serving entities based on their remaining net-short positions.
Also in January 2026, the PJM Board announced its decision on a Critical Issue Fast Path (CIFP) process addressing large load issues in PJM, which, among other things, included accelerating a backstop capacity procurement.
In March 2026, the White House released the Ratepayer Protection Pledge to assure that new large loads will, at a minimum, “build, bring, or buy the new generation resources and electricity needed to satisfy their new energy demands, paying the full cost of those resources.”  Many utilities, cooperatives, data center developers, and governors have signed the pledge.
In April 2026, the PJM Board issued a letter initiating a targeted CIFP process      to engage stakeholders in the development of the RBP.  Soon after, PJM proposed a two-path mechanism for the RBP:  a central procurement path (i.e., the RBP auction of the instant filing) and a facilitated bilateral contracting matchmaking path that PJM states requires no filing with the Commission.  PJM plans to run this latter path in parallel with the RBP auction to streamline direct contracting between supply and demand.  According to the PJM Board, bilateral contracting is “highly preferred among members.”
In June 2026, PJM issued a bilateral matchmaking request for proposals, with responses due July 21, 2026, at which time consultant Charles River Associates commenced the bilateral matchmaking process.  This process is intended to be iterative and will continue for six to nine months.  Supply-side resources in the bilateral matching process that do not form agreements may bid into the RBP auction.  Bidders will not      be permitted to then exit the RBP auction process to enter bilateral arrangements, but supply-side resources that are not selected in the RBP auction may re-engage in bilateral matching.
On May 27, 2026, PJM announced the results of an April survey to gauge interest from load in the RBP.  PJM states that the response revealed substantial large load interest from 21 entities representing 47 potential large load projects in the PJM Region; those projects average 850 MW each, with a median size of 300 MW.  PJM explains that the supply-side response was also significant, with 397 potential supply-side projects by 87 entities and approximately 136 GW in total potential capacity.  Of the supply-side projects, 72% indicated a readiness to engage with their large load counterparts immediately, while 91% of the large load projects indicated the same.
On June 30, 2026, the Members Committee voted on 13 RBP auction proposals as an advisory to the PJM Board.  Stakeholders endorsed only one proposal, meaning that it received at least two-thirds sector-weighted support.  That support (75%) went to a proposal sponsored by the Data Center Coalition (DCC) and a coalition of Electric Distributors.  PJM’s own proposal received only 30% support.  The DCC/Electric Distributors coalition proposed a “subscription model” in which large loads wishing to participate would provide their LSE with a MW volume for PJM to purchase on their behalf.  PJM instead proposed to base its procurement target on the shortage in the 2028/2029 BRA and to allocate costs to Electric Distributor zone/areas pro rata based    on forecasted load adjustments.  In addition, the DCC/Electric Distributors coalition’s proposal included a locational constraint that allowed only 500 MW to serve the        Mid-Atlantic Dominion reserve sub-zone, which was intended to prevent future         BRA price separation due to RBP resources being electrically separated from data centers.  PJM’s proposal had no locational constraints.  Despite these differences,      many of the core components of the two proposals were the same, including resource commitments up to the 2042/2043 delivery year, requiring a resource in-service date     by the 2032/2033 delivery year, a must-offer RPM requirement with contracts for differences, and similar new supply qualifications, shortfall penalties, and supplier collateral requirements.
On July 14, 2026, PJM announced that the 2028/2029 BRA cleared short of the PJM Region’s reliability requirement (when also accounting for FRR resources) at a clearing price at the temporary price cap of $325/MW-day.
On July 27, 2026, the PJM Board announced that it had adopted PJM’s proposal with three “targeted changes” to adopt certain concepts that had roots in the DCC/Electric Distributors coalition’s proposal.  First, the PJM Board added two RBP opt-outs:  one that applies to qualifying cooperatives and municipal utilities, and one that applies to Electric Distributor zone/areas that are addressing their capacity needs through state peak shaving adjustment programs.  Second, the PJM Board proposed to cap the MW-weighted average cost of accepted supply offers at $555/MW-day.  Third, the PJM Board added stringent LSE collateral requirements to address potential defaults on the demand side.  The PJM Board explained that it did not adopt the DCC/Electric Distributors coalition’s entire proposal because a voluntary subscription framework would not provide sufficient assurance that the RBP would procure enough capacity.
Filing
On July 31, 2026, PJM submitted revisions to the Tariff and RAA to establish the RBP, a one-time procurement of new capacity to address resource adequacy challenges primarily driven by an influx of large loads.  According to PJM, the goal of the RBP is   to obtain commitments of new RBP UCAP MW from eligible new resources, called RBP Resources, for a fixed term of up to 15 years, starting with the 2028/2029 delivery year at the earliest and ending no later than the 2042/2043 delivery year.  PJM states that committing supply for terms of up to 15 years creates revenue certainty for the supply resources, generally can reduce financial and development risk, and may improve financing opportunities through lower capital costs or more favorable financing terms. 
Participants in the RBP are:  (1) sellers with RBP Sell Offers submitted on    behalf of RBP Resources; and (2) PJMSettlement, Inc., acting as a counterparty on behalf of buyers, i.e., LSEs.  PJM states that the RBP aims to procure capacity equal to the 6,831 MW shortfall in the 2028/2029 BRA (Initial RBP Target), adjusted downward to reflect qualifying new capacity (Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW) serving new load and certain qualifying Electric Distributors that elect and meet requirements to opt out of the RBP (Opt-Out UCAP MW).  The Final RBP Target is the Initial RBP Target after downward adjustments.  Pursuant to the proposed Tariff provisions, new load is load that has an executed electric service agreement or transmission service agreement indicating that the load will come online during the 2027/2028 or 2028/2029 delivery year.  
To avoid double procurement, PJM proposes to require all available committed RBP UCAP MW to offer into the RPM Auctions as a price-taker, i.e., $0/MW-day UCAP, beginning with the first RPM Auction following the RBP commitment, for the applicable offered delivery year in which the term of the committed RBP UCAP MW begins and continuing each subsequent delivery year through the end of the fixed term.  All RBP Resources clearing in the RPM are paid RPM Auction Credits in accordance with RPM rules and are then settled based on a contract-for-difference design for the RBP UCAP MW.  All load that is allocated RBP Charges and participates in the RPM     is charged or receives RBP Charges, based on the contract-for-difference settlement.  RBP Credits and Charges are only assessed to the extent that RBP UCAP MW are committed in the RPM and physically available for dispatch in the relevant delivery year.
PJM states that if the Commission accepts its filing without significant revisions, PJM commits to opening the RBP bid submission window on September 30, 2026, and closing it three weeks later on October 21, 2026.  PJM states that a clearing and selection process would follow and conclude six weeks after the closing of the offer submission window.  PJM states that it would announce the pay-as-bid results to sellers a few days before the 2029/2030 BRA opens on December 9, 2026.  PJM also commits to post publicly the aggregate MW procured and a MW-weighted average of the cost.
PJM states that “to facilitate Commission approval and prompt opening of the RBP procurement window, PJM consents to the Commission’s exercise of authority to modify and/or sever the proposed Tariff and RAA language, as needed and permitted under section 205 of the FPA and NRG Power Marketing, LLC v. FERC, where such modification and/or severance is consistent with PJM’s overarching objectives in this filing,” and asks only that the Commission “expressly prescribe the revised rate or rule in its order.”
Notice of Filing and Responsive Pleadings
Notice of PJM’s filing was published in the Federal Register, 91 Fed. Reg. 50826 (Aug. 6, 2026), with interventions and protests due on or before August 21, 2026.  Notices of intervention and timely-filed motions to intervene were submitted by the entities listed in Appendix B to this order.  Comments and protests were submitted by numerous entities, as summarized below.  Answers were submitted by AEP, the Kentucky Attorney General, EKPC, the Market Monitor, NJBPU, NOVEC, Voltus, PJM, P3, PPL, Constellation, Indicated PJM TOs, and FirstEnergy.  Additional answers were submitted by Constellation and EKPC.
Discussion
Procedural Matters
Pursuant to Rule 214 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure,        18 C.F.R. § 385.214 (2025), the notices of intervention and timely, unopposed motions   to intervene serve to make the entities that filed them parties to this proceeding.
Rule 213(a)(2) of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. § 385.213(a)(2) (2025), prohibits an answer to a protest or answer unless otherwise ordered by the decisional authority.  We accept the answers filed by AEP, the Kentucky Attorney General, EKPC, the Market Monitor, NJBPU, NOVEC, Voltus, PJM, P3, Constellation, PPL, Indicated PJM TOs, and FirstEnergy because they have provided information that assisted us in our decision-making process.
Substantive Matters
Our preliminary analysis indicates that, while some aspects of PJM’s proposal are just and reasonable, other aspects of PJM’s proposal have not been shown to be just and reasonable and may be unjust, unreasonable, unduly discriminatory or preferential, or otherwise unlawful.  PJM’s filing raises issues of material fact that cannot be resolved based on the record before us and that are more appropriately addressed in the paper hearing procedures established below.  Accordingly, we accept PJM’s proposal for filing and suspend it for five months to become effective February 28, 2027, subject to refund and to the outcome of paper hearing procedures.  Specifically, the paper hearing procedures should address the Commission’s potential modifications with respect to the portions of PJM’s existing RBP proposal that are discussed immediately below.  Aside from the three issues discussed directly below, we find that the other aspects of PJM’s RBP proposal are just and reasonable, as discussed in this order.
We direct PJM to submit an initial brief addressing the paper hearing topics discussed below (cost allocation, Transmission Owner exit rules, and LSE collateral requirements), and to discuss in that brief whether its proposal could be just and reasonable if modified.  Other parties to this proceeding may also submit initial briefs    on these topics.  Initial briefs are due 45 days from the date of this order.  However,       we anticipate that the Commission would grant a motion to hold that briefing in this proceeding in abeyance if PJM submitted a new section 205 filing within 30 days from the date of this order.  Absent any such abeyance, responses to those initial briefs are due 20 days after the date that initial briefs are due.  No additional answers or briefs will be permitted, and the Commission will look with great disfavor on any requests to extend these deadlines.  Any evidence included with the briefs shall be submitted in the form     of affidavits accompanying the briefs.  We remind parties that their pleadings in Docket No. ER26-3380-000 remain part of the record in this proceeding and that they need not—and should not—repeat their prior arguments in the paper hearing.
We anticipate that, following the paper hearing, the Commission may need to direct significant modifications to certain aspects of PJM’s proposal pursuant to its authority under section 205(e) of the FPA and Western Resources, Inc. v. FERC.  
Pursuant to Western Resources, the Commission may “transform” an existing  FPA section 205 proceeding into an FPA section 206 proceeding and “impose its own rate,” provided the Commission makes three requisite findings:  (1) that the utility has failed to show that the proposed rate is just and reasonable, (2) that the existing rate is no longer just and reasonable, and (3) that the substitute rate established by the Commission is just and reasonable.  We anticipate that, based on the record developed through the paper hearing, the Commission may find that each of these three prongs is satisfied and impose a new rate that incorporates some of the potential modifications discussed below.  We first discuss why PJM’s existing rate may be unjust and unreasonable, then turn to why each aspect of PJM’s proposal that we are setting for paper hearing may be unjust and unreasonable, and then discuss why PJM’s proposal may be just and reasonable if modified.  
In addition to establishing paper hearing procedures under FPA section 205,       this order also establishes a new FPA section 206 proceeding in anticipation of the Commission directing significant modifications to certain aspects of PJM’s RBP   proposal following the paper hearing.  We institute this FPA section 206 proceeding because, as discussed in the next section below, PJM’s existing Tariff may be unjust and unreasonable.  When the Commission directs modifications under Western Resources,     it does so by “transform[ing]” an existing section 205 proceeding into a section 206 proceeding and making the requisite findings.  Though we are establishing an FPA section 206 proceeding today (Docket No. EL26-108), we are not instituting any further process under FPA section 206 at this time. 
While the Commission is establishing the procedures described above, we strongly encourage PJM to address the issues discussed in this order by submitting an alternative proposal pursuant to its FPA section 205 filing rights without delay.  Such a filing could expedite the resolution of the concerns that we have identified with certain aspects of PJM’s RBP proposal.  Should PJM submit a filing under FPA section 205, it should explain how its proposal resolves the concerns discussed in this order.
PJM’s Existing Tariff May Be Unjust and Unreasonable
We preliminarily find that PJM’s existing Tariff may be unjust and unreasonable because the existing reliability backstop provisions appear to be insufficient to prevent the grave resource adequacy concerns that led PJM to file the instant proposal in the first place.  We think it clear that PJM’s ordinary instrument for procuring sufficient capacity to meet PJM’s reliability requirement, the RPM, has failed to keep pace with the unprecedented influx of large load into the PJM Region in recent years.  
The existing Reliability Backstop Auction provision in PJM’s Tariff may be unjust and unreasonable because it has failed to remedy these reliability concerns.  As PJM states, the Reliability Backstop Auction, which was proposed over 20 years ago and has never been used, was not designed to respond to the circumstances surrounding PJM’s current capacity shortfall.  The Reliability Backstop Auction is triggered after three consecutive BRAs clear with a total unforced capacity amount that is more than one percent below PJM’s reserve margin.  As stated above, PJM’s last two BRAs have cleared more than five percent below PJM’s reserve margin.  Moreover, once the Reliability Backstop Auction is triggered, PJM cannot run the auction until it “make[s] a filing with FERC for approval to conduct a Reliability Backstop Auction.”    
The aspects of the existing Reliability Backstop Auction discussed above call into question the sufficiency of the current Tariff mechanism to adequately respond in a timely manner to the magnitude of the resource adequacy challenges that the PJM Region faces today.  We therefore conclude on a preliminary basis that the existing Reliability Backstop Auction Tariff provisions may be unjust and unreasonable.
Certain Aspects of PJM’s Proposal Are Just and Reasonable
Seller Eligibility Requirements, Sell Offers, and RPM Must-Offer Requirement
Filing
Like offset capacity, RBP Resources (i.e., resources that bid into the RBP auction) must have never cleared in an RPM Auction and must have an expected in-service date by June 1, 2032.  PJM, however, states that because RBP Resources have longer-term commitments and price certainty—as compared to resources that provide offset capacity—PJM proposes more restrictive criteria for RBP Resources to limit them to those resources that have demonstrated a high likelihood of success in reaching commercial operation in the near term and remaining available throughout the commitment period.  Thus, some categories of resources eligible to be offset capacity cannot be RBP Resources, including resources that increase UCAP by switching fuels and ELCC class but do not bring on new ICAP.  Similarly, any incremental capacity created by new Capacity Interconnection Rights (CIRs) must also be associated with an increase in ICAP.  PJM states that resources relying on Surplus Interconnection Service to provide new UCAP MW do not qualify because these resources do not have any independent rights to the PJM system.  PJM explains that, by design, a surplus resource can only operate while the existing resource is in service, or no more than one year after the deactivation of the existing resource, and when the existing resource is not operating and using the interconnection service.  PJM states that given the 15-year term of the RBP commitment period, resources need to be able to operate independently to provide certainty of deliverability for a 15-year term.  Finally, Demand Resources and DER Aggregators without identified sites and a 15-year agreement in place cannot be RBP Resources. 
Each RBP Sell Offer must include:  (1) the quantity (MW (UCAP)) to be provided by the RBP Resource for each delivery year where the maximum UCAP included in an RBP Sell Offer shall be limited to no greater than 120% of the resource type’s most recent maximum Preliminary ELCC Class Ratings for 2028/2029 delivery year through the last posted delivery year or based on the resource’s maximum estimated unit-specific ELCC ratings across such period for resources with no ELCC Class Rating, multiplied by the resource’s ICAP; and (2) the price in $/MW-day UCAP for each delivery year beginning with the first full delivery year in which the RBP UCAP MW is expected to provide capacity through the 2042/2043 delivery year.  PJM states that the 120% quantity cap reflects the fact that a resource’s Accredited UCAP value may change from year to year.  PJM argues that allowing sellers to offer amounts greater than the UCAP determined through current ELCC modeling allows sellers to offer their expected UCAP levels in future years while limiting the risk of overestimated expected UCAP values.  PJM argues the cap represents a reasonable balance between providing the seller with flexibility and managing UCAP risk for load.
Sellers are responsible for all actual Network Upgrade costs as determined through the interconnection process, without any subsequent adjustments to RBP Sell Offers.  Sellers reflect in their RBP Sell Offers the anticipated cost of any Network Upgrades, estimated or final, associated with the RBP Resource’s provision of capacity.
To avoid double procurement, PJM proposes to require a committed RBP Resource to offer its available capacity, up to the total quantity of committed RBP UCAP MW,   into the RPM Auctions as a price-taker, i.e., $0/MW-day UCAP, beginning with the first RPM Auction following the RBP commitment, for the applicable offered delivery year in which the term of the committed RBP UCAP MW begins and continuing each subsequent delivery year through the end of the fixed term.  All RBP Resources that offer and clear in the RPM are paid RPM Auction Credits in accordance with RPM rules, and then are settled based on the contract-for-difference design for the RBP UCAP MW.  All load that is allocated RBP Charges and participates in the RPM will likewise be charged RPM Charges and be charged or receive RBP Charges, based on the contract-for-difference settlement.  PJM states that RBP Credits and Charges are only assessed to the extent that RBP UCAP MW are committed in the RPM and physically available for dispatch in the relevant delivery year.
Responsive Pleadings
The Market Monitor is critical of several aspects of PJM’s proposed eligibility requirements for RBP Resources.  To begin with, the Market Monitor faults PJM’s proposal for not matching the duration of supply with the duration of data center demand, which is 8,760 hours per year.  The Market Monitor argues that because a four-hour battery is eligible to be an RBP Resource, there is a significant mismatch between the supply of energy from the battery and the demand for energy from data centers, plus the charging demand of the battery.  The Market Monitor states that the same issue exists for standalone solar resources.  According to the Market Monitor, the result of this mismatch will be higher energy prices for all PJM customers because PJM will need to dispatch higher-cost resources to meet energy demand.
The Market Monitor maintains that permitting Demand Resources and DER Capacity Aggregation Resources to serve as RBP Resources creates capacity that is materially inferior to Generation Capacity Resources.  The Market Monitor states that committed generation is required to participate in PJM’s day-ahead energy market and make itself available for economic dispatch.  In contrast, the Market Monitor asserts, committed Demand Resources are only available when PJM invokes emergency procedures.  The Market Monitor argues that this is analogous to permitting RBP offset capacity to classify its committed ICAP as maximum emergency, requiring PJM to invoke emergency procedures to access its reliability benefit.
The Market Monitor contends that PJM’s proposed qualifying criteria for RBP Resources include uprates, Demand Resources, and DER Aggregation Resources—even though the goal of the RBP should be to support new generation and to prevent gaming of the rules by reclassifying existing capacity resources as new.  The Market Monitor argues that the definition should instead ensure that all cleared capacity represents investment in new physical supply rather than redefining existing resources.
AEU, on the other hand, argues that proposed eligibility rules for Demand Resources and DER Aggregation Resources present unnecessary barriers to entry.  For example, AEU notes that, under the proposal, every site backing a commitment must be locked in before the resource can bid, for a term length that few demand-side commercial agreements can support.
JCA argues that PJM’s proposal to accept only commitment terms that terminate in the 2042/2043 delivery year excludes resources that can energize in time for the 2028/2029 delivery year but are unwilling or unable to be bound through the 2042/2043 delivery year.  JCA notes that the Charles River Associates Survey Results showed that 21% of responding suppliers would agree to terms of 10 years or less.  JCA asserts that PJM’s only support for the 15-year payout period is that it is needed to comply with the NEDC/PJM Governors’ Principles.  JCA contends that it is also unduly discriminatory to require some ratepayers to pay for 15-year procurements when other ratepayers are insulated from RBP Charges due to offset capacity with terms of only five years.  According to JCA, PJM’s assertion that a five-year contract is sufficient to satisfy the RBP’s short-term reliability need cannot be squared with a proposal requiring 15-year commitments to meet the same need.
In response, PJM argues bilateral arrangements for new capacity are distinguishable from the RBP procurement mechanism.  PJM contends that parties entering into bilateral arrangements are not similarly situated to either the suppliers offering into the RBP or the LSEs that are allocated cost responsibility for RBP UCAP MW, as bilateral arrangements are privately negotiated business deals.  PJM states that because bilateral arrangements remain the preferred approach to meeting the resource adequacy shortfall, establishing less stringent terms for offset capacity encourages parties to enter into bilateral arrangements and, thus, decrement the RBP procurement target and reduce the quantity of UCAP MW that would otherwise be subject to the more interventionist RBP framework.  PJM states that it intends the 15-year term to motivate supply to participate in meeting the procurement shortfall in a timely manner where other measures have failed.  
Parties take various stances on PJM’s proposal to require RBP Sell Offers to include the quantity of UCAP to be provided for each delivery year where the maximum UCAP included is limited to no greater than 120% of the resource type’s most recent maximum Preliminary ELCC Class Ratings for 2028/2029 delivery year through the last posted delivery year or based on the resource’s maximum estimated unit-specific ELCC ratings across such period for resources with no ELCC Class Rating, multiplied by the resource’s ICAP.  AEU asserts that PJM’s proposal unreasonably places “unhedgeable ELCC risk” on suppliers and advocates that the risk be shifted to the RPM Auctions, which would lower RBP bids.  Equinix, on the other hand, supports PJM’s proposal, arguing that load contracting today cannot price accreditation risk 15 years forward, and that a floating credit would transfer to load a modeling risk it has no ability to manage.
The Market Monitor argues that the proposed ELCC-related rules would permit generators to sell more capacity than they have and to do so without penalty for overstating capacity.  The Market Monitor argues that allowing RBP Sell Offer UCAP MW values up to 120% of the maximum preliminary ELCC class rating for 2028/2029 through the last posted delivery year will overstate the RBP cleared MW and “require customers to pay for nonexistent capacity.”
Constellation, NRG, and Policy Integrity argue that PJM’s proposal to require RBP Resources to offer into the RPM Auctions as price-takers will likely suppress RPM prices, leading to premature generator retirements and artificial shortages.  Constellation asserts that these price-formation and reliability risks are most acute when RBP Resources enter the RPM Auctions before the associated demand materializes, even if that demand eventually materializes.  In response, PJM asserts that the Commission has consistently rejected the position that requiring resources that are procured outside of a capacity market to offer into the capacity market as price-takers would unjustly and unreasonably distort or suppress capacity market clearing prices.  PJM argues that the Commission has consistently found that the interest in avoiding double-payment outweighs the concern of potential price distortion or price suppression.  PJM contends that Constellation and NRG’s positions effectively recycle arguments previously made with respect to reliability-must-run resources that have been consistently and summarily dispatched by the Commission.  PJM also argues that RBP Resources should not be excluded from capacity auctions because it could artificially inflate RPM clearing prices or require loads to be double charged for capacity.  In response, P3 asserts that reliability-must-run contracts are localized, short-term measures and therefore are fundamentally distinct from RBP capacity which involves long-term multi-gigawatt     new generation.  P3 avers that applying this to RBP will expand a limited construct, compounding market disruption and undermining market efficiency and resource adequacy across PJM.  P3 and Constellation argue that PJM does not consider the context of the Commission’s decision to require reliability-must-run units to participate as price-takers, including that it was time-limited to two auctions to avoid sustained disruption to the market.  P3 requests that the Commission modify PJM’s proposal, defer action on this matter to a future proceeding, or establish a paper hearing.
NRG argues that the Commission should impose a price floor on offers to   prevent price distortion in the event the expected load does not materialize.  In response, PJM argues that there will be a price floor that will apply to all resources offering into the RPM through the 2029/2030 delivery year and that a further extension of the price floor would be an impermissible attempt to expand the Minimum Offer Price Rule.
Constellation contests PJM’s proposal to exclude from the RBP an existing Energy Resource that has no CIRs but is seeking new CIRs through an Interconnection Request, even if the resource otherwise satisfies the RBP eligibility criteria.  Constellation explains that an existing Energy Resource necessarily has an existing Maximum Facility Output—not a “new Maximum Facility Output,” as required by PJM’s proposed eligibility rules—and obtaining new CIRs does not create a new Maximum Facility Output.  Constellation asserts that the relevant attribute from a resource adequacy perspective is the new CIRs.  Constellation concludes that excluding an otherwise eligible resource because its Maximum Facility Output is not “new” and because it is currently not a capacity resource but is seeking to obtain new CIRs is unjust and unreasonable.  In response, PJM argues that the requirement that generation RBP Resources have a new Maximum Facility Output and new CIRs ensures that eligible resources meet stringent standards before receiving 15 years of price certainty.  
PJM states that it has identified a typographical error in proposed Tariff, Attachment DD, section 18.5(d).  PJM states that the section erroneously requires   DER Capacity Aggregation Resources to meet the requirements in section 18.5(b), which is the provisions for “Generation or Energy Storage Resources as an RBP Resource.”  Rather, PJM states, PJM’s intent was to refer to the general requirements for all resources, in Tariff, Attachment DD, section 18.5(a), “RBP Seller Eligibility to Participate and General Requirements for Resources Supporting RBP UCAP MW.”    PJM therefore requests that the Commission permit PJM, on compliance, to revise the proposed Tariff language to replace the reference to section 18.5(b) with section 18.5(a).
Determination
As a general matter, we find that PJM has demonstrated that its proposed eligibility requirements for RBP Resources are just and reasonable.  Specifically, we agree with PJM that its proposed eligibility requirements will limit RBP Resources to those resources that have demonstrated a high likelihood of success in reaching commercial operation and remaining available throughout the RBP commitment period, while not being so restrictive as to foreclose significant auction participation.  We further find that the stringency of the eligibility requirements for RBP Resources is reasonable given the revenue certainty that they will obtain over the RBP commitment period should they clear the RBP auction.  
We disagree with the Market Monitor that PJM should have attempted to match the duration of supply with the duration of data center demand.  The same energy must-offer requirements apply to RBP Resources based on their resource type as would apply to any other resource of that type that cleared the RPM Auctions.  Similarly, we disagree with the Market Monitor’s arguments that uprates, Demand Resources, and DER Aggregation Resources should not be eligible RBP Resources.  The Commission has dismissed similar arguments from the Market Monitor in the context of the RPM.
We acknowledge AEU’s concern that few Demand Resources and DER Aggregation Resources can lock in their customers for 15 years, as PJM’s proposal  would require for them to qualify as RBP Resources.  We find, however, that PJM’s proposal is nonetheless reasonable.  As PJM explains, in return for the revenue certainty that participating in the RBP auction will provide, it is reasonable to expect these resources to be available during the entire RBP commitment period.  Like any other resource type, Demand Resources and DER Aggregation Resources that cannot commit themselves through the 2042/2043 delivery year are not eligible to participate in the RBP as RBP Resources, but—as is the case today—they continue to have the opportunity to participate in PJM’s routine RPM Auctions.  We also disagree with JCA that PJM cannot reasonably propose to terminate all RBP Resource commitment terms in the 2042/2043 delivery year and should instead allow for shorter commitment terms.  We note that this requirement aligns with PJM’s proposed clearing mechanism, described below, which we find to be just and reasonable.
We are unpersuaded by Constellation’s argument that PJM’s proposal to exclude generation resources that could provide new CIRs, but no new installed capacity, is unjust and unreasonable.  On the contrary, we agree with PJM that the RBP price certainty of up to 15 years should be used to attract both new installed capacity and new CIRs.  
We find just and reasonable PJM’s proposal to require RBP Sell Offers to include the quantity of UCAP to be provided for each delivery year where the maximum UCAP included is limited to no greater than 120% of the resource type’s most recent maximum Preliminary ELCC Class Ratings for 2028/2029 delivery year through the last posted delivery year or based on the resource’s maximum estimated unit-specific ELCC ratings across such period for resources with no ELCC Class Rating, multiplied by the resource’s ICAP.  We agree with PJM that the proposed cap represents a reasonable balance between providing sellers with flexibility and managing UCAP risk for load.  Under PJM’s proposal, load pays for only RBP capacity delivered.  Thus, the only risk is that PJM procures 20% more capacity on paper than what eventually materializes.  We are not persuaded that such potential harm renders this component of PJM’s proposal unjust and unreasonable.  Instead, we find an actual procurement that may result in up to 20% less capacity than the estimated target to be acceptable in the context of an estimated resource adequacy shortfall of 6,831 MW, particularly as compared to the total MW of capacity that cleared in PJM’s 2028/2029 BRA. 
We also disagree with arguments against PJM’s proposal to require RBP Resources to offer into the RPM Auctions as price-takers because the requirement        will likely suppress RPM prices, leading to premature generator retirements and    artificial shortages.  As PJM notes, the Commission has consistently found that   Regional Transmission Organizations and Independent System Operators can reasonably require resources that are compensated outside of the capacity market because they are needed to maintain reliability to offer as price-takers in capacity auctions to avoid double procurement, even at the risk of price suppression.  Here, where PJM is proposing to procure RBP Resources outside of its routine RPM Auctions because those auctions have failed to secure sufficient capacity to meet the PJM Region’s reliability requirements, we find that it is likewise just and reasonable to require RBP Resources to offer into PJM’s RPM Auctions as price-takers to avoid the risk of over-procuring capacity through those auctions.
Finally, we acknowledge PJM’s request that the Commission exercise its discretion to correct a typographical error in proposed Tariff, Attachment DD, section 18.5(d).  If PJM were to choose to expeditiously submit an FPA section 205 filing, PJM may decide whether to include that proposed revision. 
Average-Price Cap and Clearing Mechanism
Filing
PJM proposes that the levelized procurement cost of all selected RBP Sell Offers not exceed a maximum willingness to pay of $555/MW-day, on a MW-weighted average basis over all delivery years of the RBP.  PJM notes that earlier this year the Commission accepted a price cap of $555/MW-day for the 2028/2029 BRA, and that but for the lower temporary price cap, the BRA would have cleared at this cap.  PJM explains that, given that the Initial RBP Target is based on the 2028/2029 BRA shortfall, PJM proposes $555/MW-day as the cap to what load will pay for RBP capacity.  PJM argues that this “budget approach” allows the RBP to manage costs while not restricting Sell Offers to a hard price cap, and allows for potentially fluctuating offers across the     15 delivery years of the RBP term.
PJM argues that the proposed maximum willingness to pay balances the need to procure capacity and maintain system reliability—recognizing that prices above the $555/MW-day cap in some delivery years may nevertheless be appropriate under scarcity conditions—with consumer protection considerations by requiring that, ultimately, the average procurement price not exceed $555/MW-day over the RBP term.  PJM further argues that a MW-weighted average provides sellers flexibility not offered by hard caps on RBP Sell Offers.  PJM argues that setting a maximum is necessary because the RBP is not disciplined by direct buy bids that explicitly express willingness to pay, and it is not reasonable to assume that load should be obligated to pay an unlimited amount for supply.  PJM argues that it is reasonable to conclude that PJM’s willingness to pay for a 15-year commitment should not exceed the amount that load would be willing to pay for a single-year commitment under the RPM framework, given the benefits to supply resources of revenue certainty and the chance to reduce financial and development risk and improve financing opportunities through lower capital costs or more favorable financing terms.  
PJM proposes to commit RBP Resources using a pay-as-bid approach, which PJM argues is more appropriate for a one-time backstop procurement than the single-clearing-price approach used in the RPM.  First, PJM argues that because the RBP is a one-time procurement, its pricing outcomes are less likely to serve as market signals.  Second, PJM notes that the RBP will not be procuring a uniform commodity because resources may differ based on commercial operation dates, Network Upgrades, and other factors.  Third, PJM states that a uniform clearing price would require PJM to normalize offers through potentially complex and subjective assumptions.
For RBP Resources to clear the auction, PJM proposes to first filter prospective resources through “gating” criteria, which PJM argues will ensure that the selected RBP Resources are those most likely to go into service and will deter speculation.  For generation and storage resources, the seller must provide:  (1) a critical path construction schedule supporting the feasibility of a commercial operation date of June 1, 2032, or earlier; (2) interconnection study information and a development timeline appropriate to its interconnection queue study process; (3) evidence of 100% site control; (4) a financing plan showing that the resource has sufficient financial backing; (5) a permitting plan showing that the developer is on track to obtain all necessary permits; and (6) evidence that the developer has or will procure the necessary major equipment.  In addition, the seller must demonstrate that it is able to develop the underlying resource by providing “[e]vidence of experience having constructed a previous project of similar size and technology or have contracted with an engineering, procurement, and construction partner with such experience.”  A seller offering RBP UCAP MW based on a natural-gas-fired resource must provide evidence of a delivering pipeline.  To the extent the resource is located outside the PJM Region, the seller must demonstrate that the resource has progressed through its host region’s interconnection study process to obtain a completed facilities study or the equivalent and, consistent with PJM’s pseudo-tie requirements, a long-term firm point-to-point transmission service, or a confirmed transmission service request with a completed system impact study, sufficient to deliver capacity to PJM’s border.
For Demand Resources and DER Capacity Aggregation Resources, the seller  must provide evidence of the locations within PJM of the load reduction and executed customer agreements or binding commitments with identified locations and customer names sufficient to cover the offered MW quantity.  The seller must also show that it will be able to effectuate the offered load reduction through evidence of an “[e]quipment procurement plan or evidence of deployed enabling infrastructure such as metering, telemetry, load control, [Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition]/dispatch systems, or DER major equipment as applicable.”
After applying the gating criteria, PJM evaluates the RBP Sell Offers based on the first delivery year offered in the RBP Sell Offer, levelized cost, and RBP UCAP MW quantity.  The proposed selection process first orders all Sell Offers based on the resource’s identified offered delivery year, and then by price, by ordering the RBP Sell Offers “in least-cost order based on the levelized cost ($/MW-day) of UCAP MW over the fixed 15-year term.”  From this stack of offers, PJM proposes to select RBP Sell Offers until the Final RBP Target is satisfied.  PJM explains that because all RBP commitments terminate with the 2042/2043 delivery year regardless of which delivery year the RBP Resource first offered, the levelized cost determination is needed for a comparative evaluation for each resource for the period between commercial operation and the 2042/2043 delivery year.  PJM explains that a levelized cost accounts for the time value of money, which is critical when evaluating contracts spanning 15-year terms, as PJM is proposing in the RBP.  PJM explains that levelized cost will be calculated as:  Levelized Cost ($/MW-day) = Net Present Value (RBP Sell Offer price * UCAP offered)/Net Present Value (UCAP offered), with a discount rate equal to 9.5% after-tax average weighted average cost of capital.
PJM explains that, in selecting resources from the offer stack, it will first look to RBP Resources expected to reach commercial operation in the 2028/2029 delivery year.  If that set of resources is insufficient to meet the Final RBP Target, then PJM will apply the selection criteria to consider all resources offered with an expected commercial operation date in the 2029/2030 delivery year, and will continue iteratively, up to          and including the 2032/2033 delivery year, until the set of offers selected meets the    Final RBP Target.  PJM further explains that, within this selection process, it will not procure a resource that results in the MW-weighted average of the levelized procurement cost exceeding $555/MW-day, meaning that it may skip over a resource with an earlier delivery year if procuring that resource would violate the maximum willingness to pay for the procurement.  If a resource is skipped because it violates the cap but a lower-cost resource is procured that then creates “room in the budget” to select that higher-offer-earlier delivery year resource, the selection process will go back to procure that resource before continuing down the rank-order of additional offers in later delivery years.  PJM explains that the selection process prioritizes earlier delivery years to address the shortfall target as soon as possible.  PJM also states that, in procuring the least-cost set of resources, it may clear an RBP Sell Offer with an offered quantity that exceeds the remaining Final RBP Target if the solution results in a lower overall cost than the alternative.  That is, PJM may exercise the option to procure more capacity than the Final RBP Target if, compared to acquiring a resource with a higher offer price that would not reach the Final RBP Target, PJM would end up paying less overall.  PJM asserts that this would result in the more economical outcome.  Relatedly, PJM notes   that because the RBP is procuring new capacity and not simply fungible UCAP MW, RBP Resources shall not be partially cleared.  Thus, PJM may clear a set of resources with a cumulative RBP UCAP MW total that does not exactly match the Final RBP Target.
Finally, PJM states that, following the conclusion of the RBP and to the extent consistent with the existing member confidentiality rules, PJM will post a report that, inter alia, provides a transparent overview of the aggregate MW that were procured through the RBP and a weighted average of the RBP Charges as soon as is practicable after the RBP is completed.
Responsive Pleadings
JCA argues that RBP’s design defeats itself by requiring the purchase of long-term resources while constraining the participation of shorter-term resources that could better align with the identified need, and that PJM has not defended the 15-year commitment term as necessary to cure the reliability shortfall.  JCA asserts that it is unjust and unreasonable to charge ratepayers for the acquisition of years of capacity that is not needed to address the reliability shortfall and serves no cost-efficiency or other economic purpose.  
Several intervenors argue that the $555/MW-day cap is too high.  JCA argues    that the $555/MW-day cap should be substantially less because 15-year price certainty reduces supplier risk and eases financing.  JCA also argues that ratepayers could pay more than $555/MW-day if any resource that bid less fails to materialize or ceases operation prior to the end of the RBP term.  JCA argues that PJM’s borrowing of Point 1 from the VRR curve is inapposite because it is a reference cost grounded in the estimated Cost of New Entry (CONE) for a combustion turbine (CT) reference resource, whereas the RBP has no reference resource or VRR curve.  OCC argues that the proposed cap is significantly higher than the clearing price in the 2028/2029 BRA of $325/MW-day at the price cap, which also reflects the scarcity conditions in that auction. E-Cubed asserts that PJM’s proposed average price cap is not just and reasonable because it is not reflective of actual costs, nor will it solve the identified capacity shortfall. NRG argues that there is no logical reason why the prices paid to individual suppliers in the RBP should be subject to a cap based on CONE for a CT when the capacity shortfall could be covered with any number of resources, including resources using different technologies or having other characteristics that cause their costs to significantly exceed those of the reference CT.  NRG states that it has a project sufficiently advanced to participate in the RBP that has costs, net of expected energy and ancillary services revenues, that are substantially greater than the $555/MW-day cap, and it would be hard to justify the time and expense of offering it into the RBP given its costs and size. OELC argues that the proposed RBP Resource selection method is not just and reasonable because it does not adequately incentivize new dispatchable generation, which is most capable of serving load during the reliability risk conditions for which the RBP is designed. Voltus argues that the proposed gating criteria for RBP Resource offers do not recognize the commercial development pathways of distributed demand-side resources. According to Voltus, requiring customer contracts before the auction removes the commercial basis on which they would be executed. On the other hand, FirstEnergy argues that the gating criteria for demand response contain a significant ambiguity, requiring only a contract or agreement evidencing a “plan or evidence of deployed enabling infrastructure,” not one demonstrating a clear and binding commitment to provide the MWs sold into the RBP.  FirstEnergy argues that the language risks treating speculative resources as equivalent to committed resources.  FirstEnergy thus requests that PJM clarify that eligible demand response resources must be supported by binding contractual commitments.
The Market Monitor argues that the RBP clearing process is not consistent with cost minimizing principles because it favors resources with a commercial operation date in 2028/2029 over resources with later commercial operation dates even when the later resources are less costly and have better reliability characteristics. CPV supports the proposal but argues that the gating criteria language requires clarification to avoid inadvertently narrowing the pool of eligible projects. CPV proposes       a correction to refer instead to an “RBP Sell Offer.”  CPV also argues that proposed section 18.5(f)(i)(2) fails to account for sellers with generation projects currently active   in PJM’s interconnection queue that have already satisfied the applicable site control requirements that are a condition of advancing through the queue.  CPV argues that requiring such developers to separately satisfy a new three-year requirement on limited notice could impose an unnecessary additional burden.  CPV proposes to clarify that proposed section 18.5(f)(i)(2) applies only “[f]or projects without an active queue position.”
PJM Answer
PJM asserts that the arguments that procuring for a fixed term of up to 15 years is unjust and unreasonable are without merit.  PJM argues that the 15-year term for RBP is intended to motivate supply to participate in meeting the procurement shortfall in a timely manner where other measures have failed.
Regarding the proposed $555/MW-day price cap, PJM notes that some intervenors argue that the cap is too high, while others argue that it is too low.  PJM highlights   that no entity that would ultimately be responsible for paying the RBP Charges raised concerns with the proposed level of the cap.  PJM also argues that the fact that some intervenors argue that the cap is too high, while others claim that it is too low, is not indicative of a flaw in the proposal but rather is an outgrowth of PJM’s concerted effort to strike an appropriate balance and find a middle ground that is just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.  Finally, PJM also argues that the revenue certainty of a 15-year term mitigates concerns that costs have risen since the periodic review that produced the $555/MW-day figure, and notes that while a handful of suppliers argue against the proposed level of the cap, others did not.
PJM responds to concerns that the proposed gating criteria are too stringent by arguing that the criteria are appropriately tailored to limit the RBP to new capacity      with a high likelihood of coming online.  PJM states that it will provide sellers the opportunity to cure PJM-identified deficiencies and anticipates working hand-in-hand with capacity resources to determine how deficiencies may be cured.  In response to arguments that the gating criteria for Demand Resources and DER Capacity Aggregation Resources specifically are overly stringent, PJM states that the difference is by design, because generation/storage resources are tied to physical assets that make it costly to exit the market early, whereas Demand Resources and DER Capacity Aggregation Resources are, by nature, contracts or agreements that are not tied to a dedicated asset.  PJM also notes that Demand Resources and DER Capacity Aggregation Resources are able to easily enter and exit the market based on economic and other business decisions.  Finally, PJM states that RBP is designed to not allow for replacement of RBP Resources so that only the RBP Resource is eligible for RBP payments, and requiring evidence that the Demand Resource/DER locations are contracted for 15 years ensures parity with generation/storage resources that participate in RBP.
PJM states that it is amenable to CPV’s suggested revision to the gating criteria requirement that Generating Facilities provide evidence of 100% site control.  PJM agrees that the term “Application” may be ambiguous in the proposed Tariff language requiring evidence of 100% site control “for a term of at least three years from the date of submission of the Application,” and clarifies that the language was intended to state that the three-year site control requirement would begin from the date when sellers submit their RBP Sell Offer, as CPV suggested.  Further, PJM states that CPV’s request to clarify that such requirement should only be applicable to projects that do not already have an active queue position is reasonable, because projects that are both already in the interconnection queue and already meet the relevant prerequisites to proceed through      the queue will have already demonstrated a high likelihood of actualization and success.  PJM believes that CPV’s suggested redlines to proposed Tariff, Attachment DD,      section 18.5(f)(i)(2) to this effect are reasonable.
Determination
As a general matter, we find that PJM has shown that its proposed $555/MW-day maximum willingness to pay and process for selecting RBP Resources in the RBP auction are just and reasonable.  We agree with PJM that a maximum willingness            to pay set at the MW-weighted average of the levelized procurement cost over the      RBP commitment term reasonably balances the need to expeditiously procure capacity in response to the PJM Region’s imminent capacity shortfall with ensuring that the average procurement price does not exceed load’s maximum willingness to pay.  We further find that in establishing the value for the maximum willingness to pay in the RBP, PJM reasonably relied on the value of the RPM price cap that the Commission accepted in January and reaffirmed in July.  We disagree with arguments that the Commission must direct PJM to adopt a value for load’s maximum willingness to pay that is based on the most recent forward prices and production costs.  Specifically, we find that using the $555/MW-day price cap for the 2028/2029 BRA—which was just approved this January and affirmed in July, as noted directly above—is a reasonable proxy of load’s maximum willingness to pay for RBP capacity.   
We agree with PJM that the proposed pay-as-bid structure for the RBP auction is reasonable.  As PJM explains, the RBP auction is not procuring a uniform product because RBP Resources may differ based on commercial operation dates and other factors.  As such, we find that it is reasonable for each RBP Resource to be paid the price that it bids when offering into the RBP auction.  We recognize that, as both PJM and protesters note, sellers are theoretically less likely to offer near their marginal costs in a pay-as-bid auction than in a single-price auction.  We find, however, that this theoretical drawback is acceptable in the context of the proposed $555/MW-day average-price cap and the Charles River Associates Survey Results indicating strong seller interest in the RBP auction.  
Moreover, we find that PJM’s proposed gating criteria for RBP Resources are just and reasonable.  These criteria, which PJM will employ as the first step in the selection process for RBP Resources, will help to deter speculative resources from bidding into the RBP auction and ensure that the selected RBP Resources are those most likely to go into service.  Regarding arguments that Demand Resources and DER Capacity Aggregation Resources cannot feasibly lock in their customers for 15 years before the RBP auction, we find that PJM has justified this requirement as reasonable.  Specifically, PJM explains that this restriction is necessary to manage the risk of the supply being available for the full term that PJM is procuring on behalf of load in the RBP.  Failing to require Demand Resources and DER Capacity Aggregation Resources to provide evidence of the executed customer agreements or binding commitments with identified locations and customer names sufficient to cover the offered MW quantity could result in such resources contracting with different loads over the life of the RBP commitment term, contrary to its purpose of providing long-term revenue certainty for RBP Resources.  Additionally, we disagree with JCA that PJM unreasonably requires commitment terms ending no earlier than 2042/2043.  As PJM explains, long contract terms create revenue certainty for RBP Resources and generally can reduce financial and development risk and may improve financing opportunities through lower capital costs or more favorable financing terms.     
PJM explains that, after applying the gating criteria, it would evaluate sell offers first based on the resource’s identified offered delivery year, then by price, until the   Final RBP Target is satisfied.  We agree with PJM that this process for selecting RBP Resources in the RBP auction reasonably prioritizes earlier delivery years to address the PJM Region’s capacity shortfall as soon as possible.  We disagree with OELC that PJM’s proposed process for selecting RBP Resources in the RBP auction is deficient because it does not value dispatchable generation’s reliability attributes beyond what PJM’s ELCC accreditation already captures because we do not find such additional valuation metrics to be necessary for PJM’s proposal to be just and reasonable.
Finally, we acknowledge PJM’s openness to adopt CPV’s suggested redlines to proposed Tariff, Attachment DD, section 18.5(f)(i)(2).  If PJM were to choose to expeditiously submit an FPA section 205 filing, PJM may decide whether to include those revisions.  
RBP UCAP MW Shortfall Charges 
Filing
PJM proposes that an RBP UCAP MW shortfall will occur when a committed RBP Resource has not reached commercial operation for the relevant delivery year for up to three consecutive years unless the RBP Resource qualifies for an exception because it is waiting on Network Upgrades.  Once an RBP Resource has achieved commercial operation, PJM proposes that RBP UCAP MW shortfall charges will end but that RBP Resources are not paid for any RBP UCAP MW not provided.  PJM proposes that RBP shortfall charges will be equal to the product of the RBP Resource’s committed RBP UCAP MW shortfall and 20% of the RBP price.  If the RBP Resource fails to provide any RBP UCAP MW after three consecutive delivery years, PJM proposes that the RBP commitment will be rescinded for the remainder of the term.  PJM states that it proposes to allow RBP Resources to retain RBP UCAP MW commitments for up to three years because a resource’s commercial operation date may be delayed even when a project is viable.  PJM argues that the limitation on RBP shortfall charges helps reduce the barrier to entry.
Responsive Pleadings
The Market Monitor contests the proposed RBP UCAP MW shortfall charges, arguing PJM inappropriately proposes to shift ELCC-related risk from generators to customers because shortfalls due to decreases in the ELCC ratings are not subject to penalties.  The Market Monitor argues that generator performance risk is an investor risk and not a customer risk, and that one of the benefits of markets is that performance risk is assigned to generators because they are responsible for unit performance.  The Market Monitor contends that the absence of shortfall charges for failure to deliver the quantity of UCAP sold shifts the ELCC accreditation risk to load, which must pay for the additional supply to cover the shortfall.
The Market Monitor also argues that PJM unnecessarily restricts the applicability of shortfall charges to a narrow reason, is vague about the timing of the charges, and unreasonably limits the charges to three years.  The Market Monitor adds that PJM’s proposed criteria for defining shortfall charges are also vague and unenforceable, and that PJM has not explained why the RBP penalties vary so significantly from the current RPM rules.  The Market Monitor states that deficiency charges under the current RPM rules are assessed due to a failure to satisfy a commitment “for any reason,” such as derates and retirements, whereas the proposed shortfall charges would only apply for commercial operation delays.  For example, the Market Monitor argues, if a generation project configuration and MW change significantly but it still achieves commercial operation by the delivery year, it is not clear whether RBP shortfall charges would apply.
The Market Monitor further argues that use of the term “commercial operation” instead of the more precise tariff-defined “commencement of Interconnection Service” limits the applicability of RBP UCAP MW shortfall charges even more so.  Also, the Market Monitor states, the term “commercial operation” is generally not a term applied   to Demand Resources and DER Aggregation Resources, and it is not clear how the shortfall charges would apply to these resource types.  The Market Monitor states that in defining the eligibility criteria for RBP Resources in proposed Tariff, Attachment DD, section 18.5(a)(i), PJM distinguishes Demand Resources and DER Aggregation Resources as being registered and under a contract to perform versus having a commercial operation date prior to June 1, 2032.  The Market Monitor argues that      PJM does not explain why this same distinction is not included in the shortfall charge provision.
The Market Monitor also contests PJM’s proposed Shortfall Penalty exception for unavailability due to delayed Network Upgrades, arguing that the proposal shifts risks from resource owners to load.
Determination
We find that PJM’s proposed RBP UCAP MW shortfall charges are just and reasonable because they will deter speculative resources from seeking to participate in  the RBP auction without creating an undue barrier to entry.  Under PJM’s proposal, an RBP UCAP MW shortfall occurs when a committed RBP Resource has not reached commercial operation for the relevant delivery year for up to three consecutive years.  RBP shortfall charges are equal to the product of the RBP Resource’s committed RBP UCAP MW shortfall and 20% of the RBP price.  We find that PJM’s proposal to assess penalties at this level, for up to three years, is just and reasonable because these penalties, along with the pay-as-bid RBP clearing price and the promise of up to 15 years of revenue certainty, will incentivize developers of RBP Resources to deliver their RBP UCAP MW.    
We disagree with the Market Monitor’s various criticisms of the proposed        RBP UCAP MW shortfall charges, including the Market Monitor’s argument that PJM inappropriately proposes to shift ELCC-related risk from generators to customers.  Under the proposal, LSEs pay RBP Charges for only the RBP UCAP MW delivered.  Thus, the risk for customers is that they end up paying for less RBP capacity than they anticipated.  However, PJM’s proposal mitigates this risk because, as discussed above, other aspects of the proposal strongly encourage RBP Resources to deliver.
We also disagree with the Market Monitor’s arguments that PJM’s proposed Tariff revisions describing the shortfall charges are impermissibly vague, and that the Commission should reject the proposed exception for unavailability due to delayed Network Upgrades.  On the contrary, we find that this exception is a reasonable approach because it removes a risk over which RBP Resources have no control.  More generally, we are not persuaded by the Market Monitor’s multiple comparisons between the proposed RBP rules and the existing RPM rules because the RBP is a stopgap measure to address the failure of the RPM to attract sufficient supply.  An intervention, almost by definition, is not going to be “consistent with PJM’s fundamental market design,” as the Market Monitor contends.
Lack of Locational Constraints and Market Power Mitigation
Filing
PJM explains that it does not propose to apply locational constraints in the RBP.  PJM states that just as the driver of the RBP is the resource adequacy shortfall at the PJM Region level, the Final RBP Target is based on a regionwide shortfall.  PJM states that while it recognizes there are locational considerations at large for resource adequacy,    and these constraints are modeled in the RPM Auctions, it is also the case that the RPM   is an annual three-year forward framework, which allows PJM to model the necessary locational parameters—Capacity Emergency Transfer Objectives (CETO) and Capacity Emergency Transfer Limits (CETL)—to accurately capture the locational needs in the capacity market.  By contrast, PJM argues, it does not project and calculate these parameters 15 years out, which is the eligible term of the RBP, because PJM does not have the information needed to determine such locational parameters for 15-year term capacity commitments.  PJM states that as a result, including locational parameters based on today’s conditions would inevitably skew the results and lead to either over-procurement or under-procurement in given zones based on nothing more than speculation as to the state of the system 10 and 15 years from now.  Moreover, PJM argues that inclusion of a speculative locational parameter at this point would ignore the fact that PJM’s interconnection process ensures the initial deliverability of new capacity to the region.  PJM also notes that, going forward, the PJM Regional Transmission Expansion Plan (RTEP) process annually studies and addresses any transmission upgrades needed to ensure the ongoing deliverability of capacity resources.  PJM states that load deliverability is also assessed as part of the RTEP process, which will identify transmission needs as load patterns change.
PJM states that it is also not proposing direct market power screens or mitigation for the RBP because, in the context of a pay-as-bid structure with a $555/MW-day cap, the effectiveness of such measures would be limited.  PJM notes that a pay-as-bid structure, unlike a single-clearing-price structure, does not allow any resource to impact the clearing price of any other resource.  In addition, PJM states, its proposed average-price cap of $555/MW-day further discipline costs by increasing the risk that high offers do not clear.  PJM states that PJM’s proposed average-price cap is similar to the existing market mitigation rules for Planned Generation Capacity Resources because PJM may reject sell offers from those resources if they exceed 140% of an average, relevant price.
PJM argues that the risk of economic withholding is limited, because the suppliers can choose whether to participate.  PJM notes that its maximum procurement target under the RBP is limited to the 2028/2029 BRA shortfall of 6,831 MW.  PJM further notes that the Charles River Associates Survey Results identified more than 100 GW     of prospective supply interested in participating in some form through this process.  PJM argues that this level of interest indicates there is available supply that will compete to secure an RBP commitment.  PJM explains that it also expanded the pool of eligible supply by permitting participation from resources capable of achieving commercial operation beyond the timeframe required for the 2028/2029 BRA.  PJM contends that under a pay-as-bid structure, such competition should exert downward pressure on procurement costs and improve the efficiency of the RBP procurement process.

PJM states that in a  pay-as-bid approach, unlike a uniform clearing price construct where sellers are expected to offer a marginal cost, sellers are more likely to offer the expected clearing price. Responsive Pleadings
Several parties criticize PJM’s RBP proposal for what it lacks.  The Market Monitor, for example, argues that the PJM RBP proposal would violate fundamental elements of the PJM capacity market design, which include the use of a single-price clearing mechanism, locational constraints, and market power mitigation rules.  The Market Monitor argues that PJM’s decision not to include locational requirements risks customers paying higher RPM prices in price-separated Locational Deliverability Areas, in addition to paying for additional transmission and higher energy prices as expensive local resources are required to serve data centers rather than the RBP Resources.
Many other parties argue that the lack of locational constraints in the RBP is unjust and unreasonable.  PIOs and JCA argue that the Commission should modify        the proposal to require that RBP Resources be sited in the same Electric Distributor zone/area as the load they serve, which would avoid costly transmission infrastructure buildout and delays.  JCA similarly contends that the absence of locational criteria for RBP procurements poses unjustified cost risks for ratepayers.  AEP avers that the lack of a locational deliverability requirement could require customers to fund RBP Resources that are not deliverable to their zone, while resources that are necessary to address local reliability needs may not be procured at all.  
JCA contends that PJM’s assertion that it does not have information needed to determine locational parameters for 15-year term capacity commitments cannot be reconciled with PJM’s intention to allocate RBP costs to zones based on their large load forecasts.  PIOs also argue that PJM’s point that it lacks the necessary information to calculate locational parameters 15 years out is flawed because PJM does have some locational information that it could use, similar to the three-year-forward forecast for the RPM.  PIOs insist that any locational considerations (even ones with a less certain projection than the three-year forecast of the RPM) will be better than none.  AEP similarly contends that PJM’s claim that it cannot predict future CETO or CETL values with precision does not eliminate the need to establish a reasonable relationship between the resources procured and the reliability benefits for which customers are charged.
Parties similarly express concerns that PJM’s proposal includes no direct market power screens or mitigation. JCA states that PJM offers no supporting evidence that the resulting procurement price will be the result of true price competition, or that the outcome will reflect the marginal cost of the resources to be procured.  JCA states that every resource eligible to offer into the RBP can bid to raise prices to the $555/MW-day average price cap regardless of its marginal cost or that of its competitors, allowing the exercise of seller-side market power.  JCA argues that PJM admits that market power concerns remain because it acknowledges bidders are most likely to offer the expected clearing price and not their own marginal cost of production.  In contrast to PJM’s statements that there is a sufficient number of potential suppliers to discipline market power concerns, JCA states that only about 80 of the 397 projects identified in the Charles River Associates Survey Results claim an ability to achieve commercial operation by the 2028/2029 delivery year and only 3% of all projects are under construction. 
JCA and NOVEC question whether PJM has accommodated sufficient competition.  According to NOVEC, the companies with the wherewithal to prepare offers on an expedited basis and accept the uncertainty risk are likely to be staffed sufficiently to gamble on whatever the RBP rules might turn out to be without detracting from their established sources of revenue and have significant market share of PJM’s existing generation.  NOVEC argues that if more time were afforded, more participants might think through ways to offer at lower rates and still be profitable.  JCA argues that not allowing commitment terms ending before 2042/2043 excludes resources that can energize in time for the 2028/2029 delivery year but are unwilling or unable to be bound through the 2042/2043 delivery year.  JCA asserts that PJM does not defend the 15-year commitment term as necessary to cure the reliability shortfall or compare the term against shorter alternatives, despite the Charles River Associates Survey Results indicating interest from resources in shorter terms.
To expedite new capacity that can address the reliability shortfall, Amazon requests that the Commission direct PJM to provide an accelerated interconnection process for RBP Resources and resources supported by executed bilateral capacity arrangements with new large loads.  DCC encourages continued interconnection and permitting reforms.  
Determination
We are unpersuaded by arguments that PJM’s filing is unjust and unreasonable because it lacks locational constraints and direct market power mitigation.  First, we find that the proposal’s lack of locational constraints does not render PJM’s overall proposal unjust and unreasonable.  Specifically, the volume of capacity that PJM will procure through the RBP auction—up to 6,831 MW—is relatively small compared with total existing supply in PJM (149 GW), so even if RBP Resources are not located in the exact same Locational Deliverability Areas as new loads, the effect of any locational constraints should be limited.  Moreover, as PJM explains, the RBP is designed to address the PJM Region’s capacity shortfall, such that it is addressing an effectively region-wide problem.  PIOs are correct that, depending on where RBP Resources choose to site themselves, significant Network Upgrades could be triggered.  But one can reasonably assume that RBP Resources will include anticipated Network Upgrade costs in their RBP Sell Offers—meaning that RBP Resources that anticipate significant Network Upgrade costs will be less likely to clear in the RBP auction.
Second, we find that the lack of direct market power screens or mitigation for the RBP does not render PJM’s overall proposal unjust and reasonable.  As PJM explains, in the context of a pay-as-bid structure with a maximum willingness to pay set at $555/MW-day, the effectiveness of such measures would be limited.  In addition, PJM’s proposed average-price cap of $555/MW-day further disciplines costs by increasing the risk that high offers do not clear.  And as PJM argues, the exercise of market power is unlikely if even a portion of the more than 130 GW of supply identified in the Charles River Associates Survey Results decides to participate and drive down prices.
