Related Provisions: Offset Capacity, Opt-Outs, and FRR Entities Exclusion
Filing
To prevent double procurement, PJM proposes to decrease the Initial RBP Target by the amount of offset capacity.  PJM proposes to credit offset capacity (converted to load MW) against an Electric Distributor zone/area’s change in forecasted load between 2026/2027 and 2028/2029 and then recalculate all the procurement targets under that Electric Distributor given that forecast change.  Any entity can report offset capacity to PJM during the bid submission window, but Electric Distributors are required to provide reports and evidence of offset capacity in each of their respective zone/areas.  PJM determines the amount by which offset capacity may reduce the Initial RBP Target based on the applicable Effective Load Carrying Capability (ELCC) Class Ratings for the 2028/2029 BRA or, where the relevant resources do not have ELCC Class Ratings, the estimated unit-specific UCAP values for such resources.  The capacity must not have previously cleared in RPM nor been previously committed in an FRR plan, as of the beginning of the RBP.  Offset capacity may be:  (1) a new build generation resource, including new resources that obtain Capacity Interconnection Rights (CIR) transferred from either deactivated resources or resources that have announced deactivation as of April 10, 2026; (2) incremental capacity created by an uprate of existing Generation Capacity Resources, but only to the extent such incremental capacity is created through an increase in such Generation Capacity Resource’s ICAP and increase in CIRs associated with that Generation Capacity Resource; (3) incremental capacity created by the use of Surplus Interconnection Service; (4) repowering of a deactivated generation resource that deactivated prior to April 10, 2026; (5) incremental capacity, whether due to greater unforced capacity or a higher level of CIRs, created by an existing Generation Capacity Resource’s changing fuel type to a more efficient fuel type; or (6) Planned Demand Resource or Planned Distributed Energy Resources (DER) Capacity Aggregation Resources.  Under these rules, Energy Storage Resources are eligible.
Offset capacity may be supported by signed bilateral contracts for at least five delivery years or by self-supply generation that is in an integrated resource plan with either associated generation in the PJM interconnection queue or signed bilateral contracts for at least five delivery years.  To serve as offset capacity, both signed bilateral contracts and self-supply must be supported by documentation of an expected in-service date of no later than June 1, 2032.  The evidence must also demonstrate that the new capacity is matched with new load.  PJM argues that the five-year requirement ensures capacity is not transitory while not being so lengthy as to undermine the flexibility needed for commercial contracting.
New load can provide offset capacity by participating as a Demand Resource or DER Capacity Aggregation Resource.  Such load must offer their full load MW quantity into the RPM Auctions starting in the 2028/2029 Second Incremental Auction and continuing through the 2032/2033 delivery year.  Such new load can subsequently replace UCAP MW provided through such participation by purchasing offset capacity that comes from eligible generation or storage resources.
The Initial RBP Target is also decremented where an Electric Distributor elects to opt out a zone/area in one of two circumstances.  First, an opt-out may be requested where the Electric Distributor’s zone/area has rates that are not regulated by the states (e.g., cooperatives or municipal utilities) and is unable to address cost allocation associated with capacity procured in the backstop.  PJM states that during the stakeholder process, cooperatives raised the concern that Electric Distributors in a retail choice state not regulated by the state and not otherwise serving as the LSE for generation to the load would be forced to have its customers absorb the costs of an “overbuy” if a forecasted large load failed to materialize.  PJM states that unlike a state-regulated, investor-owned utility, cooperatives and municipal utilities are not governed by a state regulatory authority that would be responsible for addressing the potential reallocation of RBP costs to either other large loads or other zones within the state.  The opt-out request must specify the associated MW quantity of load in the zone/area that will be opted out of the Initial RBP Target and be accompanied by supporting documentation demonstrating an inability to address cost allocation associated with capacity procured in the backstop, along with written support for such opt-out from the relevant state governor, RERRA, and interconnection customer(s).  Second, an Electric Distributor may also request to opt out of the RBP for up to the associated MW quantity of load that participates in a peak shaving adjustment program codified in state law, where an Electric Distributor’s zone/area addresses its capacity needs through such a program.
Finally, PJM explains that FRR Entities are excluded from the Initial and Final RBP Targets as well as the RBP overall.  PJM argues that the FRR, by design, is an opt-out of RPM, and the RBP is curing a resource adequacy gap from which FRR load and FRR capacity are already removed.

PJM’s Proposal May Be Unjust and Unreasonable
For purposes of determining whether a proposed cost allocation method is just and reasonable, both “[the Commission] and federal courts have long understood the [FPA’s] just-and-reasonable requirement ‘to incorporate a cost-causation principle.’”  Under the cost causation principle, all Commission-jurisdictional rates and charges must “reflect to some degree the costs actually caused by the customer who must pay for them,” and costs must be allocated in a manner that is at least roughly commensurate with benefits.  Compliance with this principle is evaluated by “comparing the costs assessed against a party to the burdens imposed or benefits drawn by that party.”  Courts and the Commission have acknowledged that adherence to the cost causation principle does not require that cost allocation methods balance costs and benefits with “exacting precision.”  Instead, the Commission may approve a given cost allocation framework if it “has an articulable and plausible reason to believe that the benefits are at least roughly commensurate with” the assigned costs.  Consistent with this longstanding precedent, we apply the cost causation principle to evaluate PJM’s proposed method for allocating RBP costs. 
As an initial matter, we find PJM’s proposal to exclude FRR Entities from the RBP to be just and reasonable, and thus we do not include it in the list of topics that will be the subject of the paper hearing procedures established in this order.  We agree with PJM that the FRR Alternative, by design, is an opt-out of RPM and that the RBP addresses a resource adequacy gap from which FRR load and FRR capacity are already removed.  FRR Entities are required to demonstrate in their FRR Capacity Plan that they have sufficient resources to meet their load obligations.  Accordingly, we find that FRR Entities have not contributed towards the resource adequacy gap that the RBP will address and, therefore, it is just and reasonable and consistent with the cost causation principle to exclude FRR Entities from being allocated costs associated with the RBP.  We disagree with protesters who argue that PJM’s proposal is unduly discriminatory against LSEs that meet their reliability requirements through self-supply.  Specifically, we find that such LSEs are not similarly situated to FRR Entities because, while both FRR Entities and LSEs that self-supply own or have contracted for the capacity needed to meet their load obligations, FRR Entities’ load and capacity are removed from RPM, while the load and self-supplied capacity of such LSEs are not.  Moreover, only FRR Entities entirely take on the risks of over- or under-supply in their own regions; LSEs that self-supply, on the other hand, continue to participate in RPM such that they can procure additional capacity or sell excess capacity in the RPM Auctions.
We find that PJM’s proposed opt-out for qualifying cooperatives and municipal utilities may be unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory.  PJM states that qualifying cooperatives and municipal utilities should be permitted to opt out of the RBP because they lack state regulatory oversight, and therefore may be unable to assign costs to specific large loads.  Because cooperatives and municipal utilities serve large loads that are similarly situated to large loads served by other LSEs, allowing an opt‑out may be unduly discriminatory.
With respect to cost allocation, as a general matter, we find that PJM’s proposed RBP cost allocation method may be unjust and unreasonable.  As discussed below, we make this finding because, based on the current record, PJM has not adequately demonstrated that its proposal is just and reasonable and consistent with the cost causation principle. 
Under the proposed tariff revisions, PJM “shall allocate the Initial RBP Target MW to each Electric Distributor’s zone/area using that zone/area’s pro-rata share of the difference between the forecasted Load Adjustments for the 2026/2027 Delivery Year and the 2028/2029 Delivery Year.”  As a general matter, allocating RBP costs to Electric Distributor zone/areas based on a “snapshot” of load growth between 2026/2027 and 2028/2029, adjusted down by qualifying offset capacity, may be just and reasonable, because it reasonably assigns costs to those responsible for the near-term capacity shortfall.  Thus, such zone/areas benefit from procurement of new resources to fill this urgent gap.  We generally find that PJM’s proposal to initially assign RBP costs to Electric Distributor zone/areas, with the ultimate cost allocation to the LSEs as determined by the state and/or RERRA and as reported to the Electric Distributor by PJM, may be just and reasonable, as it reflects the authority of PJM under the Tariff and respects the authority of the states and/or RERRAs.  However, we agree with concerns in the record that relying on Load Adjustments to measure load growth may be inconsistent or not reasonably capture forecasted load growth or actual large load growth; thus, PJM’s method for allocating RBP costs may be unjust and unreasonable.  
Specifically, based on PJM’s explanation in a previous proceeding of the way in which it avoids double counting when accounting for Load Adjustments, and comments in this record, it appears some large loads may never have been accounted for as Load Adjustments because PJM accounted for them when calculating the initial load forecast.  In short, the delta accounts for net load growth associated with any size or type of load, while excluding any new large loads that PJM knew of and accounted for when calculating the initial load forecast.  As such, the Initial RBP Target MW may only capture a portion of new load growth, potentially leaving out some new large loads.  This could lead to the costs imposed on certain entities not being at least roughly commensurate with the benefits they will receive from the procurement.  
As discussed above, while a cost allocation method need not allocate costs with “exacting precision,” in order to be just and reasonable it must allocate costs in a manner that is at least roughly commensurate with benefits.  We find that a cost allocation method that results in fixed cost assignments over the 15-year RBP commitment period that is based on accurate load forecast information may be just and reasonable and consistent with the cost causation principle.  However, PJM has not demonstrated that reliance on the Load Adjustment process is just and reasonable.  The RBP is a one-time procurement of capacity resources to address a shortfall attributable to load growth in certain Electric Distributor zone/areas.  Allocating RBP costs based on a snapshot of this shortfall over the term of the RBP commitment period may provide greater certainty to the LSEs in the Electric Distributor zone/areas ultimately bearing responsibility for those costs. 
Having found that PJM’s proposed method for allocating RBP costs among Electric Distributor zone/areas may be unjust and unreasonable, and because we are ordering paper hearing procedures to examine a reasonable cost allocation method, we decline to further address arguments raised in the protests related to PJM’s proposed cost allocation method at this time.
PJM’s RBP Proposal May Be Just and Reasonable if Modified 
Having found that PJM’s proposed RBP cost allocation method may be unjust and unreasonable, and having also initiated an investigation into PJM’s existing Tariff under FPA section 206, we now conclude that additional record evidence is needed to determine whether PJM’s proposed RBP cost allocation method could be just and reasonable if modified.  We therefore establish paper hearing procedures and direct further briefing on the issues discussed below.  However, we note that the Commission encourages PJM to carefully consider the issues we raise in this order and determine the most expeditious path to resolving them.  In particular, we encourage PJM to consider swiftly submitting a new FPA section 205 filing without delay.  
While we find that PJM’s proposal to allocate RBP costs based on its Load Adjustment process may be unjust and unreasonable, we note that it may be just and reasonable for PJM to allocate RBP costs based on updated load forecast information.  PJM could base the RBP allocation on the difference between the actual load for 2026/2027 delivery year in each Electric Distributor zone/area with the most recent 2028/2029 delivery year load forecast for each Electric Distributor zone/area.  This could ensure that the load forecast information on which the allocation relies reasonably captures all forecasted load growth.  Such a method for allocating RBP costs among Electric Distributor zone/areas may be consistent with the cost causation principle because it would appropriately assign RBP costs to the Electric Distributor zone/areas with the reported new load that is driving the need for the procurement.  Similarly, PJM should employ the most up-to-date load and resource forecasts to inform the Initial RBP Target.
We reiterate that we encourage PJM to swiftly submit a new section 205 filing without delay.  We anticipate that the Commission would grant a motion to hold the briefing in this proceeding in abeyance if PJM submitted a new section 205 filing within 30 days from the date of this order.  However, absent such an FPA section 205 filing, initial briefs are due 45 days from the date of this order.  Briefs should address whether the above-described method for allocating RBP costs would be just and reasonable.  
We recognize that the rapid emergence of large loads presents a shared regulatory challenge that implicates both federal and state authority.  Under the FPA, the Commission oversees rates and practices affecting wholesale service, including PJM’s procurement of capacity through the RBP.  However, “states determine how Commission-approved rates are collected among the relevant retail consumers along with the rates for state-jurisdictional matters.”  Specifically, states have authority over how the wholesale costs of providing electricity, including transmission of such electricity to the retail customers, are recovered through retail rates.  We are encouraged by the NEDC/PJM Governors’ Principles, in which the governors of all 13 PJM states agreed to “[u]se all available authorities to ensure that their state public utility commissions design rate class structures to ensure that their states’ LSEs allocate their share of the cost to procure new capacity through the [RBP] to new data center loads that have not otherwise procured capacity or agreed to be curtailable.”  We are also encouraged by the execution of the President’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge, through which data center developers have committed to shield retail ratepayers from increased electricity prices.  Our partners in the states are more than capable of ensuring that these promises reach fruition.  While we appreciate and take seriously the issues that PJM’s RBP proposal is designed to address, as well as the concerns surrounding the unprecedented influx of large loads more broadly, having only such powers as are given to us by Congress, we will not pretend that all of these issues can be solved exclusively by market design in the federal sphere.  The PJM states have their own role to play.
Transmission Owner Exit Rules
Filing
PJM proposes to set forth the responsibilities of various parties in the event a Transmission Owner exits from PJM.  PJM states that establishing these rules in the RBP proposal will provide the requisite notice of how RBP commitments will be honored and recognizes that a primary incentive for developers to participate in the RBP is the revenue certainty afforded developers through a 15-year commitment.  PJM’s proposal is described below.
First, if a Transmission Owner exits PJM and committed RBP Resources are physically in that Transmission Owner’s service territory, the Transmission Owner may, prior to exiting PJM, enter into a separate agreement with the impacted RBP Resources that would maintain appropriate rates, terms, and conditions of the RBP commitments.  If the exiting Transmission Owner does not enter into such an agreement, PJM proposes to require the exiting Transmission Owner to cover all costs necessary for those RBP Resources that exceed the Transmission Owner’s withdrawn load to be pseudo-tied back into PJM pursuant to Tariff, Attachment DD, section 5.5A, thus allowing such resources to continue providing capacity to serve PJM’s load.  PJM states that RBP Resources would be exempted from the electrical distance test to allow for such resources to be pseudo-tied back into PJM, which will allow such resources to qualify as external capacity resources that can continue to serve PJM loads even if such resources are physically located beyond the usual electric distance requirement.  In the event PJM does not elect to retain such RBP Resource or the resource is unable to be pseudo-tied back into PJM, the exiting Transmission Owner would be obligated to pay for the remaining term of the RBP Resource’s commitment on an accelerated basis prior to exiting PJM as determined through a separate filing with the Commission.  In the latter two cases, PJM states it would pay the collected revenues from the Transmission Owner to the impacted RBP Resources.
Second, if a Transmission Owner withdraws from PJM and net load leaves with the Transmission Owner, resulting in stranded committed RBP Resources remaining within the PJM Region, PJM similarly proposes to allow such exiting Transmission Owner, prior to exiting PJM, to enter into agreements that would maintain appropriate rates, terms, and conditions and preserve the RBP commitments with the owners of the RBP Resource(s).  Absent such an agreement, PJM proposes to require the Transmission Owner to pay for all forward obligations associated with the net load that was allocated RBP Charges, the exact amount which would be determined through a separate filing with the Commission.  PJM argues that this would ensure that the remaining load within the PJM Region will not be stranded with increased costs necessary to pay for the remaining term of RBP Resources that are not located within the Transmission Owner’s service territory.  PJM states that the revenues collected from the Transmission Owner and credited to remaining loads will help offset any cost increases to remaining loads that may be necessary to continue honoring the commitments of RBP Resources remaining in the PJM Region through the rest of the 15-year term.
PJM states that establishing these rules in the Tariff now avoids any potential arguments that changes to cost allocation associated with the RBP Resources after the commitments have already made may be impermissibly retroactive.  PJM adds that these rules predominately affect RBP Resources and load commitments, particularly in relationship to how they interact with other obligations and assurances provided by suppliers and buyers, and are thus properly addressed in the Tariff, as part of the rules concerning the RBP framework.

PJM’s Proposal May Be Unjust and Unreasonable
We find that, as proposed, the Transmission Owner exit provisions may be unjust and unreasonable.  
As protesters note, the Commission has previously found that it is just and reasonable to impose generation capacity costs on LSEs located within an exiting Transmission Owner’s zone.  In Duquesne, the Commission assessed a withdrawing LSE’s RPM obligations and noted that “[u]nder RPM, PJM is responsible for procuring capacity on behalf of LSEs in each zone three years in advance based on the auction results, and PJM’s obligation to pay the generators is fixed at the time of the auction.”  The Commission stated that “Duquesne understood that PJM was procuring capacity on its behalf and therefore should be obligated to pay for that capacity.”  Under its RBP proposal, PJM similarly proposes to procure capacity through the RBP on behalf of LSEs, establish obligations to pay RBP Resources at the time of the procurement, and later allocate those costs to LSEs.  PJM fails to explain why Transmission Owners—who are not the buyers for which PJM procures capacity under the RBP—should be responsible for RBP Charges.  
Based on the current record, it appears that the proposed Transmission Owner exit provisions may be inconsistent with the cost causation principle because they do not assign costs to the entities that cause the costs and benefit from the capacity procurement under the RBP, i.e., LSEs.  As explained in Section IV.B.3.a.i(d) above, under the cost causation principle, all Commission-jurisdictional rates and charges must “reflect to some degree the costs actually caused by the customer who must pay for them,” and costs must be allocated in a manner that is at least roughly commensurate with benefits.  Here, it appears that PJM has not demonstrated that the proposed obligations and “exit fees” associated with RBP costs—which PJM proposes to impose on the exiting Transmission Owner—reflect the benefits that the RBP will provide.  PJM’s RBP proposal is necessary to address capacity shortfalls in the PJM Region, and the beneficiaries of the RBP are the LSEs on whose behalf PJM will procure capacity through the RBP.  Therefore, we find that PJM’s proposed exit provisions may be unjust and unreasonable because they would assess RBP Charges to exiting Transmission Owners, rather than the LSEs in the relevant Transmission Owner’s zone.  
However, we disagree with protesters that establishing exit provisions in the Tariff would unnecessarily constrain the parties involved in effectuating a Transmission Owner’s withdrawal from PJM.  As PJM states, the cost obligations will be “appropriately decided at the time of Transmission Owner’s exit and subject to Commission approval.”  
PJM’s RBP Proposal May Be Just and Reasonable if Modified
As a general matter, we recognize that it may be just and reasonable to have provisions to protect against cost shifts should a Transmission Owner exit PJM during the RBP term (i.e., before the end of the 2042/2043 delivery year).  As discussed above, the Commission has found that a withdrawing LSE’s obligations under the RAA and Attachment DD of the Tariff may include capacity costs.  Similar to the costs of capacity that PJM procures through its RPM Auctions, PJM here proposes to allocate the costs of procuring capacity through the RBP to LSEs.  Therefore, a just and reasonable approach could require LSEs in an exiting Transmission Owner’s zone to pay RBP exit fees commensurate with their cost allocation under the RBP, to prevent cost shifts to other LSEs in the PJM Region.  As PJM proposes, exit provisions could still leave flexibility for LSEs to enter into agreements with RBP Resources (which they may need to serve their load) or pay to pseudo-tie RBP Resources located within the exiting Transmission Owner’s zone back into PJM.  
As discussed elsewhere, we conclude that additional record evidence is needed to determine a just and reasonable approach to preventing RBP cost shifts should a Transmission Owner exit PJM before the end of the 2042/2043 delivery year (i.e., the completion of the term of RBP Resources’ commitments).  Among other topics, the Commission directs further briefing on whether (1) it would be appropriate for LSEs in an exiting Transmission Owner’s zone to be responsible for RBP exit charges, rather than the Transmission Owner, and (2) it would be just and reasonable to assign LSEs RBP exit charges based on the cost of capacity that PJM procures through the RBP on behalf of LSEs in a Transmission Owner’s zone, i.e., the LSE’s cost allocation under the RBP.
LSE Collateral Requirement
Filing
PJM proposes to require both RBP Sellers and buyers of RBP UCAP MW (i.e., LSEs) to provide collateral.  The collateral for RBP Sellers, required to be posted at the time of the auction, reflects three years of RBP UCAP MW shortfall charges for that resource.  PJM returns the collateral when an RBP Resource no longer gives rise to credit exposure (e.g., after the resource fails to clear).  The RBP collateral requirement for LSEs is the product of the RBP Credit Rate and the total RBP MW committed.  PJM explains that the initial RBP Credit Rate of $1.5 million ensures that PJM holds sufficient collateral to cover about 50% of the notional value of all RBP commitments.  PJM proposes to require that LSEs post collateral 45 days before the first delivery year in which RBP Resources are expected to be in service (i.e., 2028/2029), and that the collateral be returned as financial exposure lessens.  Citing elevated risks in the current marketplace, PJM also proposes strict criteria for acceptable collateral.  PJM states that, “like the credit requirements imposed on inherently riskier Financial Transmission Rights,” sellers and buyers of RBP UCAP MW are limited to providing RBP Collateral in the form of either a cash deposit or Letter of Credit. 
If an LSE defaults and fails to pay an RBP Charge, the defaulted amount is reallocated to all remaining LSEs responsible for paying RBP Charges based on their pro rata share of the total RBP Charges for all such LSEs.  Such amounts may be offset by the RBP Collateral posted by the defaulting LSE.  If an RBP Resource defaults on payment of RBP shortfall charges, the corresponding credits are not allocated to the LSEs that would otherwise receive them.
Responsive Pleadings
Parties contest both the proposed RBP Collateral requirement for LSEs and the proposed criteria for acceptable collateral.  FirstEnergy, for example, faults PJM’s proposal for several reasons, arguing that PJM’s filing lacks the support typically provided for credit requirements.  FirstEnergy also faults PJM’s proposal for assuming all classes of LSEs present the same credit risk, regardless of whether they have regulated cost recovery.  FirstEnergy contends that the proposal is also unduly discriminatory because under similar Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act contracts, the purchasing entities generally have been subject to low or no collateral requirements because of their ability to recover costs from retail customers.  
EKPC argues that PJM has not linked the RBP collateral requirement to exposure, as evidenced by (1) the timing gap between when the exposure is identified and when the collateral is required and (2) the misalignment between the buyer collateral requirement and the seller collateral requirement.  EKPC contends that PJM’s proposal would result in the same obligation being collateralized twice, once under RBP and once under Attachment Q of its existing Tariff.  EKPC argues that it is also unjust and unreasonable to require LSEs to post collateral prior to the finalization of the cost allocation because it does not provide LSEs with sufficient transparency and time to challenge the obligation.  EKPC asserts that it is not just and reasonable to concentrate the collateral requirements among LSEs that receive RBOs because this creates system liquidity risk.
SMECO notes that LSEs could have as few as 15 days from the time they learn their final collateral requirement to the deadline to post that collateral.  This is the case because the deadline for Electric Distributors to report RBO allocations is 60 days before the delivery year, while the collateral deadline is 45 days before the same delivery year.
Equinix argues that the RBP Collateral requirement for LSEs is not just and reasonable for three reasons.  First, Equinix asserts that the collateral requirements are disproportionate and inconsistent because sellers have the most control over risks of development and non-performance but have lower collateral requirements than buyers.  Second, Equinix disagrees with PJM that RBP exposure is analogous to FTR exposure because the latter is volatile while RBP Charges are fixed in advance, which is similar to the risk PJM manages under Attachment Q of its existing Tariff.  Third, Equinix argues that the collateral requirement does not protect ratepayers because it will require LSEs to finance the posting of the collateral, which will materially raise rates.  Equinix requests that the Commission modify the proposed buyer-side RBP Collateral provisions so that collateral is calibrated to reasonably foreseeable forward exposure and the forms of credit support available under Attachment Q are permitted.
NOVEC argues that its highest possible collateral requirement, estimated to be about $1.95 billion, would exceed NOVEC’s total assets and disrupt NOVEC’s ordinary business operations.  NOVEC adds that it is uncertain whether it would even be able to secure $2 billion in collateral.  NOVEC argues that PJM’s proposal to require the collateral obligation of the buyers to span the entire 15-year period is not necessary, as the risk could be significantly mitigated by a shorter period, such as three years.  NOVEC contends that the most significant obstacle to NOVEC fulfilling its RBP obligations is the size of the RBP collateral obligation itself and not the RBP Charges.  NOVEC notes that PJM’s proposal limits the RBP Sellers’ collateral obligation to three years to avoid making the collateral requirement “onerous.”  
NOVEC and Constellation also take issue with the assumptions PJM makes when calculating the initial RBP Credit Rate of $1.5 million.  NOVEC and Constellation argue that PJM’s calculation assumes that RBP buyers have to collateralize the entire $555/MW-day, when the RBP Charges will be the RBP clearing-price average (which can be less than $555/MW-day) net of revenues from the capacity auction.  EKPC and Constellation aver that PJM has sized collateral as though load owed the full contract price, when the Tariff obligates load to pay only a difference between two prices under the contract for differences approach.  Effectively, NOVEC argues, RBP buyers are providing collateral to ensure that everyone in PJM pays the capacity costs associated with the RBP Resources.  NOVEC notes that RBP buyers themselves already provide PJM collateral to ensure that they pay their capacity rates under Attachment Q, and so do all other capacity buyers.  NOVEC argues that PJM is thus requiring duplicative collateral.  Constellation also expresses concerns that (1) the credit rate relies on 15 years of gross contract value rather than the net RBP Charges that LSEs will be billed; (2) the Tariff does not identify the time needed to draw collateral and reallocate any residual default, or the stress assumptions used to estimate net exposure; (3) it applies the same $1.5 million/MW base rate without explaining why credit quality may increase—but never reduce—the base requirement; and (4) the Tariff establishes no mandatory recalculation schedule, prescribed inputs, or objective collateral-release standard.  
NOVEC further argues that the proposed Tariff provision is ambiguous as to when the collateral obligation will be reduced and does not appear to properly reduce it over time.  NOVEC notes that according to the proposed Tariff provision, “the RBP Credit Rate shall equal $1.5 million, as may be reduced, for reasons including a change in the total committed RBP UCAP MW, when total posted RBP Collateral is greater than the total remaining RBP Charges obligations, over time by the Office of the Interconnection to an amount sufficient to cover the total existing RBP Charges obligations.”  NOVEC argues that PJM should not have the discretion to determine whether RBP buyers should be required to post more collateral than the total existing RBP obligations, especially given that the calculation already overstates the likely RBP Charges.  NOVEC further argues that there are too few circumstances in which the collateral obligation is reduced.  According to NOVEC, if PJM believes that 50% of the total payment obligations at the start of the 15-year term is sufficient, then the same percentage of the total remaining payment obligations should be the cap for each year.
AEP asks the Commission to direct PJM to clarify that collateral obligations attach only to LSEs allocated responsibility for RBP Charges, not to Electric Distributors acting solely in an administrative or delivery-service role.  AEP argues that this clarification would be consistent with PJM’s statement that RBP Buyer collateral is intended to mitigate the risk of non-payment of RBP Charges and that only LSEs allocated responsibility for RBP Charges generally will have a credit requirement.  AEP further argues it would be inconsistent with the cost causation principle to improperly shift credit risk from the entities serving and benefiting from the load to an Electric Distributor that neither controls generation supply decisions nor receives the revenues associated with serving that load.
PPL states that it understands that if there are no RBOs reported to PJM for an Electric Distributor zone/area with RBP UCAP MW assigned, or if there are “stranded” RBOs, then the credit requirements will move to all LSEs in the zone/area based on Peak Load Contributions.  Presumably, PPL continues, once credit requirements are assigned based on Peak Load Contributions, RBP Charges will also flow to those LSEs.  EKPC and PPL are concerned that this scenario could result in LSEs that do not serve large loads receiving these obligations, thereby having nowhere to assign them except to other customers.  EKPC, ODEC, and PPL request that PJM clarify that if an LSE defaults and fails to pay an RBP Charge, whether the defaulted amount will be allocated to all remaining LSEs in the Electric Distributer zone/area or to all LSEs in the PJM Region.  
Constellation recommends that large load customers be permitted to post collateral for the responsible LSE to avoid unnecessary intermediation through the LSE and duplicative credit postings.  Constellation states that the record is not sufficiently developed to prescribe a durable collateral methodology and requests that the Commission establish an expedited paper hearing on the matter.
Answers
PJM argues that imposing a credit requirement for the purpose of ensuring only those entities assigned cost responsibility for RBP Resources bear the burden of such costs protects those LSEs not allocated cost responsibility for RBP Resources from having to pay for such resources.  
In response to protesters’ claims that the proposed LSE collateral requirement is duplicative of exiting PJM credit rules, PJM argues that its existing requirements (i.e., Peak Market Activity collateral) serve a different purpose and tracks different types of financial exposure than the proposed RBP credit requirement.  PJM states that the Peak Market Activity metric manages immediate, rolling operational risk from daily transactions based upon a rolling, backward-looking billing history, and to the extent an LSE defaults on its obligations, the provider of last resort for that load becomes responsible on a going-forward basis.  In contrast, PJM states that the proposed RBP credit requirement is to cover forward-looking risk over a long-term, up-to-15-year commitment to sellers.  PJM also argues that an LSE’s obligation to pay RBP Charges should not be shunted to a provider of last resort because the large load driving the need for RBP should bear these costs.
In response, NOVEC maintains PJM’s proposal does require suppliers to provide duplicative collateral because PJM proposes to determine RBP collateral obligations as if suppliers were paying the entire RBP Charge—which means suppliers are providing collateral for the cost of capacity of their RBP MW and providing collateral for the RBP clearing price, and not just for the difference between the RBP price and the capacity clearing price.
Regarding protests that the credit requirements should be tailored to the credit risk presented by specific LSEs, PJM states that it looked at the forward obligation to the RBP Resources instead of individual LSE’s creditworthiness because (1) it better safeguards the payment and reduces exposure in case of default, (2) it allows for a uniform credit rate applicable to each allocated MW, which ensures non-discriminatory requirements for all LSEs, and (3) creditworthiness of individual LSEs may change considerably during a 15-year term.
In response, NOVEC argues that PJM overstates the risk of declining creditworthiness because the RBP Charges that NOVEC could be responsible for represent, in any given year, a tiny fraction of the collateral PJM would require NOVEC to post.  NOVEC therefore argues that the greatest threat to NOVEC’s credit rating is PJM’s own RBP collateral requirement.  
In response to protesters’ claims that the credit requirements are excessive, PJM argues that the credit requirements are properly tailored to mitigate the risk associated with RBP commitments throughout the up to 15-year RBP commitment term and therefore is derived from the measured forward exposure of the RBP Charges.  PJM asserts its approach is consistent with Commission policy because it reasonably balances protecting PJM’s members against the risk of default and appropriately correlating the credit requirement with the risk level.  PJM adds that it limited the forms of collateral to letters of credit and cash because it determined there would likely not be sufficient unsecured credit available from these LSEs to cover the up-to-15-year forward credit obligation.  PJM argues that the initial RBP Credit Rate of $1.5 million per RBP UCAP MW is just and reasonable and supported because it is keyed to a potential outcome of the RBP, the maximum MW-weighted average of the levelized procurement cost of all selected RBP Sell Offers of $555/MW-day, and represents about 50% of the notational contract value at that price.  PJM contends that this represents approximately 50% of a quantifiable potential contractual exposure, rather than full collateralization, and can decline as the remaining exposure declines, which undermines claims that the amount is excessive or insufficiently correlated to credit risk.  PJM argues that protesters ignore the fact that standard business practices for LSEs signing up new large loads include requiring collateral.
PJM clarifies that the LSE collateral requirement for a delivery year is based only on RBP UCAP MW committed for that delivery year and that “no collateral would be required for RBP Resources [that] are not in service for that Delivery Year, and no RBP Charges would be assessed.”  In response, NOVEC argues that PJM’s interpretation relies on the meaning of the term “committed” used in proposed Tariff, section 18.8(b)(i)(A).  NOVEC points out that proposed section 18.6(e) permits a resource to remain “committed” for up to three delivery years, and proposed section 18.8(b)(i)(A) does not have an “in-service” limitation, creating the risk that NOVEC could post collateral for an RBP Resource that does not operate during those three delivery years.  NOVEC asks the Commission to require PJM to revise this section to state that LSEs with RBP obligations will not be required to post collateral for RBP Resources that are not in service.  
PJM states that, while it has proposed a just and reasonable approach to determining the proper buyer-side LSE RBP credit requirement, it also consents to a modified approach where the credit rate is keyed to the actual MW-weighted average of the levelized procurement cost of all selected RBP Sell Offers that results from the RBP and not the maximum of such value.  PJM states that it would consent to the Commission resolving the applicable buyer-side LSE RBP Credit Rate through additional procedures.
PJM’s Proposal May Be Unjust and Unreasonable
First, although it is related to the broader topic of RBP Collateral, we find PJM’s proposed collateral requirements for RBP Sellers just and reasonable, and thus we do not include that aspect of the proposal in the list of topics that will be the subject of the paper hearing procedures established in this order.  Specifically, PJM’s proposed collateral requirements for RBP Sellers are just and reasonable because they will reduce the risks to PJM markets associated with non-payment of RBP Shortfall Charges without posing an unreasonable barrier to market participation.   
However, we find that the proposed RBP Collateral requirement for LSEs (i.e., LSE Collateral requirement) may be unjust and unreasonable.  
PJM proposed an initial credit rate of $1.5 million per committed RBP MW because it would collateralize approximately 50% of the estimated contractual value associated with RBP commitments.  However, as FirstEnergy notes, PJM does not support its 50% estimate with any quantitative measures, including an expected probability of default, a loss-given-default assumption, a historical LSE default experience, a liquidation or replacement period, or any other quantitative measure.  PJM also fails to demonstrate how the LSE Collateral requirements strike a reasonable balance between protecting PJM’s markets and its members against the risk of default and ensuring that market participants have adequate flexibility to manage their collateral requirements.  PJM otherwise provides little flexibility for LSEs to manage their collateral requirements, including a short timeline for posting collateral and limited, acceptable forms of collateral.  Taken together, we find that PJM’s proposed LSE Collateral requirements may be unjust and unreasonable because they do not strike a reasonable balance between protecting PJM’s markets and its members against the risk of default and ensuring that market participants have adequate flexibility to manage their collateral requirements.
PJM’s RBP Proposal May Be Just and Reasonable if Modified
We find that additional record evidence is needed to determine if PJM’s proposed LSE Collateral requirement is just and reasonable.  Therefore, as discussed elsewhere, we establish paper hearing procedures and further briefing on appropriate collateral requirements for RBP buyers.  As part of their responses, parties should address (1) what initial RBP Credit Rate is appropriate and (2) whether 45 days before the start of the delivery year is sufficient time for LSEs to post collateral.

Filing and Responsive Pleadings

EL26-108-000
As stated earlier, we are establishing a new FPA section 206 proceeding in Docket No. EL26-108-000.  In cases where, as here, the Commission institutes a section 206 investigation on its own motion, section 206(b) of the FPA requires that the Commission establish a refund effective date that is no earlier than the date of publication by the Commission of notice of its intention to initiate such proceeding nor later than five months after the publication date.  In such cases, in order to give maximum protection to customers, and consistent with our precedent, we have historically tended to establish the section 206 refund effective date at the earliest date allowed by section 206, and we do so here as well.  That date is the date of publication of notice of initiation of the section 206 proceeding in Docket No. EL26-108-000 in the Federal Register.

As we are setting the section 206 proceeding in Docket No. EL26-108-000 for further proceedings, we expect that we would be able to render a decision within five months of the date of this order.

SWETT, Chairman, concurring:

American ratepayers and utilities need urgency, clarity, and discipline—none of which PJM appears capable of delivering at this time.
